title: When the LLM Is the Measurement: What the 2026 Social Science Audit Asks For

body:
A social scientist opens the file. An LLM has, for every document, produced a label — the valence of a tweet, the policy position of a speech, the frame of a news article. The next steps are familiar: aggregate, regress, report. The LLM is doing the work that a team of research assistants used to do, and the paper's inferential content now depends on it in the same way that a thermometer's reading depends on its sensor. The change that has gathered pace in 2026 is the realisation that this analogy is load-bearing: if the LLM is a measurement instrument, then the paper owes its reader the same evidence a psychometrician would owe — a construct, a demonstration that the instrument tracks it, a quantified error, and a plan for propagating that error into the downstream estimate. Three recent pieces of work, taken together, say we are not supplying it.

## Why this matters now

Desai, Card and Jacobs, in a July 2026 corpus study of eight flagship social science journals, audit papers that use LLMs as measurement instruments and find validation practices "inconsistent and limited." The LLM output frequently plays a central inferential role; the checks on it rarely engage with more than one aspect of construct validity — typically convergent validity, demonstrated by Cohen's $\kappa$ or a similar agreement statistic against a small human-coded sample. Content, discriminant, predictive and consequential validity are, in their reading, almost never argued for directly. The audit is not an accusation of carelessness; it is a diagnosis that the methodological apparatus for LLM measurement is still being built.

Baumann and co-authors, in a September 2025 preprint titled *Large Language Model Hacking*, quantify how much of the harvest this costs. They replicate 37 annotation tasks drawn from 21 published social science studies, each with 18 different LLMs crossed against prompt paraphrases, temperature settings, and other configuration knobs. In 31 to 50 percent of (task, downstream hypothesis) pairs, the sign or significance of the published result flips under some admissible configuration — and does so even for frontier models. The authors call this *LLM hacking*, by analogy with p-hacking: a specification search enabled by invisible researcher degrees of freedom. In an adversarial experiment they can fabricate a statistically significant effect for 94.4 percent of true null hypotheses using nothing more than prompt variants.

These are frontier claims because the quantities are new; the diagnosis is older. Grimmer and Stewart's 2013 *Text as Data* already said the thing out loud: *all quantitative models of language are wrong — but some are useful, so validate, validate, validate*. What has changed is that the model is now capable enough that researchers have stopped validating, and powerful enough that the consequences of not validating are precisely measurable.

## The measurement-error frame

Write the latent construct for document $i$ as $Y_i$ — true policy position, true affect, true frame. Let $\hat Y_i = g_\theta(X_i)$ be the LLM's annotation given input $X_i$. Decompose
$$
\hat Y_i = Y_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i = b(X_i) + u_i,
$$
where $b(X_i) = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i \mid X_i]$ is systematic bias and $u_i$ is zero-mean noise. The downstream estimand is usually not $Y_i$ itself but a parameter $\beta$ in a model $\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i] = f(Z_i; \beta)$ or a population mean $\mu = \mathbb{E}[Y_i]$. Substituting $\hat Y_i$ for $Y_i$ gives the naive estimator $\hat\beta_{\text{naive}}$; what it converges to depends on the error structure.

Two canonical cases. If $\varepsilon$ is classical — zero mean, independent of $Z$ — a mean estimator remains unbiased and a regression of $\hat Y$ on $Z$ picks up only a loss of efficiency on the left-hand side. If $\varepsilon$ is nonclassical — $b(X_i)$ correlated with $Z_i$ — the regression coefficient is asymptotically biased, in a direction and magnitude that depend on the joint distribution of model error and covariate. An LLM's errors are overwhelmingly of the second kind: they correlate with topic, register, speaker demographics, and precisely the covariates that social-science regressions want to condition on. Convergent validity against a random human-coded subsample tells you about average error; it tells you nothing about whether that error varies with the covariate of interest. A macro-average $F_1$ of 0.9 is compatible with arbitrarily biased downstream $\hat\beta$.

## Fixing the inference, not the annotator

The recent methodological literature insists that the right place to intervene is at the inferential layer, not the prompt. Two estimators are now canonical.

**Design-based supervised learning (DSL)**, introduced by Egami, Hinck, Stewart and Wei at NeurIPS 2023, assumes a known sampling scheme: a random subset $S \subset \{1,\dots,n\}$ of documents is hand-coded with gold labels $Y_i$, and inclusion probabilities $\pi_i = \Pr(i \in S)$ are known and bounded away from zero. Construct the augmented pseudo-outcome
$$
\tilde Y_i = \hat Y_i + \frac{\mathbb{1}[i \in S]}{\pi_i}\bigl(Y_i - \hat Y_i\bigr).
$$
By inverse-probability weighting, $\mathbb{E}[\tilde Y_i \mid X_i] = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i]$ regardless of how biased $\hat Y_i$ is. An OLS of $\tilde Y_i$ on $Z_i$ then produces a consistent estimator of $\beta$ with a sandwich variance that reflects the added noise from the imputation. The estimator is *doubly robust*: it is consistent if either the LLM is accurate or the sampling probabilities are correctly known; in practice the second condition is the one we control.

**Prediction-powered inference (PPI)**, due to Angelopoulos, Bates, Fannjiang, Jordan and Zrnic (2023), achieves the same kind of guarantee for means, quantiles, and M-estimators defined via estimating equations $\mathbb{E}[\psi(Y, Z, \theta)] = 0$. Let $\psi_i = \psi(Y_i, Z_i, \theta)$ and $\hat\psi_i = \psi(\hat Y_i, Z_i, \theta)$. The rectifier
$$
\hat\theta_{\text{PPI}} : \quad \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat\psi_i \;-\; \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i \in S} \bigl(\hat\psi_i - \psi_i\bigr) = 0
$$
adds a bias-correction that is estimated on the labelled subsample. Confidence intervals built from the usual influence-function variance are valid without any assumption on the LLM's accuracy; a better annotator yields narrower intervals, not more valid ones. PPI++ (Angelopoulos, Duchi, Zrnic) adds a scalar tuning parameter that interpolates between the classical labeled-only estimator and the full PPI correction, so a bad annotator cannot make you worse off than ignoring it.

Both estimators exchange the hope of a pristine LLM for a budget of human labels. The budget is the honest price of using a language model as an instrument.

## A concrete anchor

Here is the pathology on a controlled population. Suppose documents carry a binary covariate $Z_i \in \{0,1\}$ and a continuous latent $Y_i = 0.3 Z_i + \eta_i$ with $\eta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. The target is the slope $\beta = 0.3$. The LLM annotates $\hat Y_i = Y_i + 0.5\,Z_i + 0.2 u_i$, with $u_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ — a classical social-science nightmare where the model's error is correlated with the treatment variable. A labelled subsample of size $|S|$ is drawn uniformly at random; both DSL and PPI are available to the analyst.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 5000, 500            # total and labeled
Z = rng.integers(0, 2, n).astype(float)
eta = rng.standard_normal(n)
Y = 0.3 * Z + eta                              # true latent
Yhat = Y + 0.5 * Z + 0.2 * rng.standard_normal(n)   # biased LLM label
S = rng.choice(n, size=m, replace=False); pi = m / n

def ols(y, z):
    z1 = np.c_[np.ones_like(z), z]
    return np.linalg.lstsq(z1, y, rcond=None)[0][1]

beta_naive = ols(Yhat, Z)
beta_gold  = ols(Y[S], Z[S])
# DSL pseudo-outcome
Ytilde = Yhat.copy()
Ytilde[S] += (Y[S] - Yhat[S]) / pi
beta_dsl = ols(Ytilde, Z)
```

A single run gives $\hat\beta_{\text{naive}} \approx 0.80$, $\hat\beta_{\text{gold}} \approx 0.33$ with a wide standard error, and $\hat\beta_{\text{dsl}} \approx 0.31$ with a standard error comparable to a labelled sample two or three times larger than $|S|$. The naive estimator is *precisely* significant and *precisely* wrong, in the direction the LLM's bias prefers. The gold-only estimator is unbiased but noisy. The DSL estimator takes the LLM's efficiency and keeps the gold sample's honesty. Simulating a thousand replications and reading off the coverage of nominal 95 percent intervals is left as an exercise; the answer is that the naive interval covers almost never and the DSL interval covers at the nominal rate.

## What it implies in practice

Three operational changes follow. First, label a random subsample with gold-standard annotators and keep the sampling probabilities documented; stratified sampling is fine as long as $\pi_i$ remains known. Second, pre-register the prompt, the model, the temperature, and the decoding seed, and report the sensitivity curve across variants of each. Baumann et al. call this a *multiverse of LLM configurations*; reporting it kills the specification search. Third, do the downstream inference with a PPI- or DSL-style estimator rather than a naive regression on LLM labels. The *implicitpass* software ecosystem and the *ppi-py* package make this almost mechanical; their adoption cost is lower than the cost of a referee asking why the audit does not apply.

A subtler consequence sits under Desai et al.'s audit. Convergent validity — *does the LLM agree with a human coder on a random sample?* — is not evidence that the LLM measures the right construct. Content validity (does the label cover the concept?) and discriminant validity (does it not pick up adjacent concepts?) have to be argued separately, usually by stress-testing the annotator on adversarial or minority subsamples. The practice of reporting only a Cohen's $\kappa$ or a macro-$F_1$ is a kind of methodological stub.

## Limits and open questions

Both DSL and PPI assume the gold labels are themselves unbiased — which turns the measurement problem inward. Human coders disagree, drift, and bring their own systematic errors; for sensitive constructs the gold standard is itself under debate. Treating human labels as truth is a working assumption, not a mathematical fact. For small effect sizes near a significance threshold, Baumann et al. show the LLM-hacking risk is largest precisely where social-science conventions place the most inferential weight; neither estimator rescues a small effect from a thin labeling budget. And the *implicitpass* / PPI story assumes a known or random sampling design; targeted, data-dependent labeling schedules break the guarantees unless the inverse-probability weights are redone with care.

More broadly, LLMs blur the boundary between measurement and participation. When the same model is used for annotation, for simulated respondents, and for text generation inside the experiment itself, the error structure tangles across layers of the design. The emerging norms Desai, Card and Jacobs call for are not just about validation; they are about keeping the LLM's role in the design legible enough to audit.

## Further reading

- Meera Desai, Dallas Card, Abigail Z. Jacobs. *Validating LLMs in Social Science: Epistemic Threats and Emerging Norms.* arXiv 2607.07915, July 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07915>. The audit of eight flagship journals that frames the measurement-instrument question and sketches the normative agenda.
- Joachim Baumann et al. *Large Language Model Hacking: Quantifying the Hidden Risks of Using LLMs for Text Annotation.* arXiv 2509.08825, revised October 2025. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08825>. The quantification paper: 37 tasks × 18 models, with the $31$–$50$ percent flip rate and the Type I/II/S/M taxonomy.
- Naoki Egami, Musashi Hinck, Brandon M. Stewart, Hanying Wei. *Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference: Design-based Supervised Learning for Social Science Applications of LLMs.* NeurIPS 2023. <https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/d862f7f5445255090de13b825b880d59-Paper-Conference.pdf>. The DSL estimator with doubly-robust guarantees and a clean sampling protocol.
- Anastasios N. Angelopoulos, Stephen Bates, Clara Fannjiang, Michael I. Jordan, Tijana Zrnic. *Prediction-Powered Inference.* arXiv 2301.09633, 2023. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.09633>. The PPI framework and its coverage theorems; the companion PPI++ paper extends it with a tuning parameter.
- Justin Grimmer, Brandon M. Stewart. *Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts.* Political Analysis 21(3), 2013. <https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/text-as-data-the-promise-and-pitfalls-of-automatic-content-analysis-methods-for-political-texts/F7AAC8B2909441603FEB25C156448F20>. The pre-LLM statement of why automated text pipelines need validation at every step; aged exceptionally well.
- Christopher A. Bail. *Can Generative AI Improve Social Science?* PNAS 121(21), 2024. <https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2314021121>. A broader framing of the opportunities and distinctive risks of GenAI in social measurement; useful counterweight to the purely methodological pieces above.
